q: When can a structure be called statically determinate?
o: When all its reactions and internal forces can be found from the equations of equilibrium alone
When it has more unknown reactions than equilibrium equations
When it needs deformation (compatibility) equations to be solved
When it has no supports that resist moment
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: A planar structure has three equilibrium equations (ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0). If those are enough to find every unknown, it is determinate. If there are more unknowns, it is indeterminate and deformation conditions must be added.

q: Compared with a simply supported beam of the same span and load, how does fixing both ends affect the beam?
o: It makes the beam more flexible, so it deflects more
It makes the beam stiffer, so the midspan deflection and moment are smaller
It has no effect on deflection, only on the reactions
It removes all bending moment from the beam
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: End fixity stops the ends from rotating. Under a uniform load, a fixed-ended beam deflects only one-fifth as much as a simple beam (wL⁴/384EI against 5wL⁴/384EI), and its midspan moment drops from wL²/8 to wL²/24, though negative moments of wL²/12 appear at the supports.

q: In what unit is the internal shear force in a beam expressed?
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: Shear is a force, so it is in kN (or N, lb). Bending moment is force times distance, kN·m. kN/m is a distributed load and kPa is a pressure or stress.

q: In the figure, which beam is an overhanging beam?
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: Beam C sits on a pin and a roller like a simple beam, but it extends past the roller. That overhang is what makes it an overhanging beam. A is a simple beam and D is a continuous beam.

q: What does a shear diagram show?
o: How the internal shear force V changes along a member
How the internal bending moment M changes along a member
How the deflection changes along a member
How the axial force changes along a column
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: The shear diagram plots V against position. Its slope equals the load intensity, and where it crosses zero the bending moment is at a maximum, which is why it is drawn before the moment diagram.

q: In the figure, which support resists horizontal force, vertical force and moment?
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: C is a fixed support: it stops the member end from moving in any direction and from rotating, so it gives three reactions in a plane (H, V and M). A pin (B) gives two forces and a roller (A) gives one.

q: What does a moment diagram show?
o: How the internal shear force V changes along a member
How the load is distributed along a member
How the internal bending moment M changes along a member
How the support reactions change with time
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: The moment diagram plots M against position. The change in moment between two points equals the area of the shear diagram between them. Its peak gives the design moment for the member.

q: Which truss analysis method isolates each joint and applies ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 to it?
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: In the method of joints, every joint is a small free body with two equilibrium equations, so you start at a joint with no more than two unknown member forces and work across the truss. The method of sections is faster when only a few members are needed.

q: In the figure, which beam is a continuous beam?
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: Beam D runs without a break over three supports. A beam that spans more than two supports is continuous and is usually statically indeterminate. It develops negative moment over the middle support.

q: What is the point of inflection (contraflexure) in a beam?
o: The point where the shear force reaches its largest value along the span
The point where the curvature changes sign and the bending moment is zero
The point where the beam deflects the most under the applied load
The point directly above a support, where the reaction acts on the beam
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: At a point of inflection the beam changes from sagging to hogging, so the moment there is zero. Continuous and fixed beams have them; a simple beam under gravity load does not. Bar cut-off points are often placed with reference to them.

q: In the figure, which beam is a propped cantilever?
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: Beam E is fixed at one end and rests on a roller at the other. It has four reactions (three at the wall, one at the roller) against three equilibrium equations, so it is statically indeterminate to the first degree. B, with no prop, is an ordinary cantilever.

q: In what unit is a bending moment expressed?
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: A moment is a force multiplied by a lever arm, so its unit is kN·m. kN/m looks similar but is a distributed load (force per length) and is a common mistake on exam sheets.

q: Which truss analysis method cuts through the members of interest and applies equilibrium to one side of the cut?
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: The method of sections cuts through no more than three unknown members and treats one part of the truss as a free body. Taking moments about the point where two of the cut members meet gives the third force directly.

q: In the figure, which beam is a simple beam?
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: Beam A spans between a pin and a roller at its two ends. Both supports let it rotate, so there is no moment at the supports and the reactions come from equilibrium alone.

q: A planar beam has four support reactions. What does that tell you?
o: It is statically indeterminate to the first degree
It is indeterminate to the fourth degree
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: A planar beam has three equilibrium equations. With three reactions it is determinate (if they are well arranged), with fewer it is unstable, and each reaction beyond three adds one degree of indeterminacy. Four reactions minus three equations leaves one. This count is only a shortcut; badly arranged supports can still be unstable.

q: Under the usual sign convention for beams, what does a positive bending moment do?
o: Makes the beam hog, concave downward, with tension at the top
Twists the beam about its axis
Makes the beam sag, concave upward, with tension at the bottom
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: By the common "smile" convention, positive moment sags the beam (concave up) and puts the bottom fibres in tension, as at midspan of a simple beam. Negative moment hogs it, as over the support of a continuous beam or at a cantilever root.

q: What happens when a simply supported beam is extended to overhang past its support?
o: The load on the overhang reduces the positive moment in the span and creates negative moment at the support
The positive moment in the span increases, and the support moment stays at zero
The support reactions become zero because the overhang balances the span
The beam becomes statically indeterminate and needs compatibility equations
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: Load on the overhang acts like a counterweight: it lifts the span, cutting the sagging moment, while hogging moment builds up over the support. An overhanging beam on a pin and a roller is still statically determinate.

q: In the figure, which beam is a cantilever?
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: Beam B is fixed at one end and free at the other. The fixed end gives all three reactions, so the beam is statically determinate, and the largest moment and shear occur at the fixed end.

q: What is needed to analyse a statically indeterminate structure?
o: Only the geometry of the structure
Compatibility (deformation) conditions as well as equilibrium
Only the loads, since the supports do not matter
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: An indeterminate structure has more unknowns than equilibrium equations. The missing equations come from how the structure must deform, for example zero deflection at a prop. Methods such as moment distribution and slope-deflection do this.

q: In the figure, which support provides only one reaction, perpendicular to the surface it rests on?
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: A is a roller. It stops movement into the supporting surface but lets the member slide along it and rotate, so it gives a single reaction. Rollers are used at one end of long beams and bridges so they can expand with temperature.

q: In the figure, which beam is a fixed-ended beam?
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: Beam F is built into supports at both ends, so neither end can move or rotate. It has six reactions against three equations, making it indeterminate to the third degree (second degree if axial effects are ignored).

q: What mainly defines a beam as a structural member?
o: It carries loads along its axis, mainly through compression
It carries loads transverse to its axis, mainly through bending and shear
It carries only tension along its axis
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: A beam spans between supports and carries loads applied across its length, which it resists by bending and shear. A column carries axial compression, and a tie carries axial tension.

q: In the figure, which support resists horizontal and vertical force but lets the member rotate freely?
ref: Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; Leet, Uang & Gilbert, Fundamentals of Structural Analysis
n: B is a pin (hinge). It gives two force reactions in a plane but no moment, because the member can rotate about the pin. A simple beam uses a pin at one end and a roller at the other.
